$schema: Evidence registry for LeanAcademy cognitive-training modules. Every module loaded into the production exercise catalog must have a matching, productionApproved entry here. See docs/evidence-review.md for full narrative writeups and docs/product-requirements.md for how evidenceLevel gates catalog inclusion.

evidenceScale.strong: Several high-quality studies/reviews with reasonably consistent results.
evidenceScale.moderate: Credible positive evidence exists, but effects may be modest or inconsistent.
evidenceScale.limited: Evidence exists but has substantial uncertainty.
evidenceScale.experimental: Interesting research exists but efficacy has not been established.
evidenceScale.unsupported: Do not use as cognitive training.

modules.population: healthy adults (young and older adults studied separately)
modules.nearTransfer: moderate — improves performance on other n-back variants and structurally similar WM tasks
modules.farTransfer: not established — no convincing evidence for fluid intelligence, general 'smartness', or everyday functioning
userFacingClaimLimits: May describe as 'improves performance on this and similar working-memory tasks'
Must NOT claim IQ increase, general intelligence gain, or everyday cognitive improvement
limitations: Many source studies lack double-blind design or pre-registration
Near-transfer measures are sometimes nearly identical to the training task, inflating apparent effects
Far-transfer literature is inconsistent across labs

modules.targetConstruct: cognitive control (response inhibition, interference resolution, task-switching)
modules.population: healthy children, adults, and older adults
modules.nearTransfer: limited and paradigm-specific — not a general property of cognitive-control training; observed between closely related interference tasks but not between response-inhibition and interference-control paradigms in the same study
modules.farTransfer: not established — a dedicated 21-day task-switching training RCT found a clean far-transfer null (no gain on fluid intelligence, working memory, response inhibition, or interference control)
userFacingClaimLimits: If shipped, must be framed strictly as within-task practice ('practice managing distraction on this task'), never as general focus/attention/impulse-control improvement
limitations: Recent RCTs show limited evidence of transfer even to nearby tasks after online inhibition training

A 2024 study found Go/No-Go training did not transfer to the closely related Flanker task, direct evidence the transfer profile is paradigm-specific rather than a general 'cognitive control' construct

Flanker/Simon/spatial-Stroop interference scores have documented weak concurrent and convergent validity across individuals, undermining their use as a reliable individual-differences outcome; no 2023-2026 rebuttal or replication found that overturns this

Task-switching training, reviewed as its own paradigm in a dedicated 2026-09-17 pass, does not clear a higher evidence bar than Flanker/Go-No-Go and stays bundled under the same decision rather than becoming a separate module
Not included in MVP catalog pending stronger transfer evidence or a clearly scoped within-task-only framing

modules.trainedTaskImprovement: supported — large effect on immediate and durable serial/free recall versus rehearsal, including in participants naive to the technique
modules.nearTransfer: supported for list/sequence recall tasks that permit spatial-imagery encoding
modules.farTransfer: not established for general memory ability outside strategy-compatible material
userFacingClaimLimits: Present as teaching a real, usable memory strategy for lists/sequences, not as a general memory-boosting exercise
limitations: 2025 systematic review rates underlying evidence quality as low-to-very-low due to risk of bias in source studies, despite consistent positive direction
Effectiveness depends on material being compatible with spatial/imagery encoding (works well for lists, less directly for abstract facts)

modules.trainedTaskImprovement: supported — modest, comprehension-preserving speed gains observed under controlled paced-reading + metacognitive training
modules.farTransfer: not established for large speed multipliers; modest gains (not doubling) are the realistic, evidence-backed target
userFacingClaimLimits: Never report a WPM change without the paired comprehension score
Never imply reading speed can be doubled without comprehension cost
limitations: 2023 RCT found training-group gains of roughly +35 WPM without comprehension loss — a modest, realistic effect size, not a dramatic one

Perceptual span (the region of text usable per fixation) is a hard physiological constraint (~3-4 letters left, ~14-15 letters right of fixation) that bounds how much speed gain is plausible without comprehension cost

The Reading Efficiency Score's comprehension floor (0.70) is sourced from Betts' (1946) Informal Reading Inventory instructional-level convention, a separate and older source than the Klimovich RCT above — that RCT establishes realistic WPM-gain size, not a pass/fail comprehension threshold

modules.trainedTaskImprovement: plausible but not strongly quantified in isolation from paced-reading training
modules.nearTransfer: limited — evidence largely inferred from perceptual-span and eye-movement literature rather than dedicated chunking-training RCTs
userFacingClaimLimits: Must explicitly state this does not eliminate normal eye movements or fixations — it practices grouping, not a new visual mechanism
limitations: Few dedicated RCTs isolate chunking practice as a standalone intervention; most evidence comes from perceptual-span/eye-movement research rather than training-outcome studies
Framed as a supplementary technique within paced-reading training, not a standalone claim of a distinct trained ability

modules.targetConstruct: reading speed via eliminated eye movements
modules.population: general readers (marketing claims largely self-reported, not independently replicated at high WPM)
modules.trainedTaskImprovement: not established at the WPM levels commonly marketed (e.g. 600 WPM)
limitations: Perceptual and cognitive 'speed limit' research indicates comprehension breaks down well before commonly marketed RSVP speeds
High-WPM RSVP comprehension claims (e.g. 80%+ at 600 WPM) are vendor self-reports, not independently replicated controlled results
Eliminating eye movements/regressions removes a mechanism (re-fixation) readers normally use for comprehension monitoring and error correction
Explicitly excluded from production per the spec's 'do not implement common speed-reading myths' principle

modules.population: healthy adult readers (general population and medical-student eye-tracking studies)
modules.trainedTaskImprovement: plausible but not isolated in any dedicated training-outcome study
modules.nearTransfer: not supported — comprehension cost is the documented mechanism of skimming, not a side effect training removes
limitations: Skimming's speed comes from deliberately processing less of the text (fewer/shorter fixations, longer saccades) — a real, well-studied mechanism, not a debunked myth like RSVP, but incompatible with an adaptively-scored exercise that must show rising speed with preserved comprehension

An adaptive skimming exercise would structurally need rising speed alongside falling comprehension as the 'successful' outcome, conflicting with the project's permanent WPM-must-carry-comprehension rule

Adjacent ESL/EFL classroom literature claiming comprehension-score gains mostly trains skimming as an exam-answering strategy (locate the answer sentence), a narrower construct than 'read an entire text quickly with preserved comprehension', and is low-rigor (small, no-control-group, single-classroom studies)

modules.population: healthy adult readers (Kaakinen & Hyönä); college freshmen (Berger 1966)
modules.trainedTaskImprovement: not established — no modern study isolates training purpose-adaptive pacing as an intervention
limitations: Purpose measurably changes reading behavior under instruction (well-established descriptively via eye-tracking), but no RCT or meta-analysis tests whether training someone to do this deliberately produces a benefit beyond natural ability or beyond the already-approved fixed-target paced-reading module

The one directly on-point outcome study (Berger, 1966) is a 60-year-old ERIC report predating modern trial standards (no randomization/blinding/pre-registration mentioned), with a mixed result even on its own terms
Hard to operationalize as a trainable, measurable exercise — reading-pedagogy sources treat it as an instructional heuristic, not a validated measurement protocol

modules.targetConstruct: working memory maintenance and updating with an arithmetic combination step
modules.nearTransfer: limited — shares the working-memory maintenance/updating mechanism with n-back and complex-span training but has no dedicated training studies of its own
userFacingClaimLimits: Present as a variant working-memory maintenance/updating practice task, not as independently validated beyond the general n-back/complex-span updating literature
Never claim improvement in general math or arithmetic ability — the arithmetic step is a fixed-difficulty response format, not a trained skill this task adapts
limitations: No dedicated training-study literature exists for this exact dice-sum/arithmetic-combination task; evidence is inherited from the broader n-back/WM-updating literature, the same reasoning already applied to running-memory-keep-track-v0

Performance may be confounded by baseline subitizing speed and addition fluency rather than working-memory capacity alone, so individual variation partly reflects a skill this task doesn't isolate or train
